Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
This is the most careful of the four documents. It reports its moderators honestly, admits where design and measurement can't be separated, uses actual hours where available, and lands on a sensible middle estimate. The internal arithmetic is consistent:
- Study counts add up across every classification.
- The prediction interval matches the pooled estimate and CI on the log scale.
- The per-hour and per-worker estimates imply plausible hours cuts of about 11–16% across subgroups.

The main problems are one clear overclaim, about duration, and two places where the evidence is presented as stronger than it is.

## 1. The duration claim isn't supported

"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" rests on a between-study comparison of four studies. That can't show what it claims:
- **Wrong comparison.** Decay is a change *within* a study over time. Comparing long studies with short ones tells you nothing about trajectories. Studies with repeated measurements should be analysed for within-study trends.
- **Survivorship.** Long follow-ups exist only where the scheme continued. Organisations that reverted, like Halden's retail firms, don't produce 24-month data, so long studies are selected toward success.
- **Uncontrolled comparison.** We aren't told the design or hours measure of the four long studies. If they are uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, +14.0% is inflated by the biases the paper has already identified. They should be compared with like-for-like short studies.
- **Imprecision.** A CI of 6.2–22.4 includes substantial decay from the corrected estimate.

The accurate statement is "too little evidence to assess durability." This sentence also appears in the abstract, which is where readers will take it from. It also undercuts the Discussion's rejection of Varga & Holm (see §6).

## 2. The "convergence" on 8–10% is largely the same studies counted repeatedly

The overlap figures in the text let you reconstruct the cross-tabulation:
- 12 of 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours. So **6 of the 8 actual-hours studies are controlled**, and only 3 controlled studies used scheduled hours.
- 9 of 14 uncontrolled studies used manager reports. So **7 of the 12 record-based studies are controlled**.

The controlled (+8.2%), actual-hours (+7.9%), and record-based (+9.7%) subgroups therefore share most of their studies. Their agreement is not independent corroboration. Reporting the intersection directly would be more informative: controlled, actual hours, *and* record-based. That is probably around five studies, including Varden. Report that estimate, its CI, and how many studies it rests on, and present it as the best estimate, with its uncertainty stated.

## 3. Small-study asymmetry may be heterogeneity, not publication bias

With I² = 81%, Egger's test and trim-and-fill are known to perform poorly, and funnel asymmetry can arise from moderators alone. Here that seems likely. Small studies are plausibly the uncontrolled pilots with manager reports and scheduled hours, which are the features already associated with larger effects.

If so, two things follow:
- Interpreting the asymmetry as selective publication isn't justified. It is also less likely given that the authors searched working-paper repositories and contacted pilot authors.
- Listing the bias-adjusted 9.1% next to the moderator subgroups as "converging" estimates partly counts the same correction twice.

Running Egger's test with the moderators included, or checking for asymmetry within the controlled studies alone, would separate the two explanations.

## 4. The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work is probably not "real" productivity

This is the same issue as in Varden's counter stratum. In queue-based work, output per hour largely reflects how much idle time staff have between customers. Fewer staff during unchanged opening hours means less idle time and longer waits, which raises contacts per hour without anyone working faster. The +6.2% is consistent with no change in work rate. The sentence "the per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate" should be reworded.

For this category, the per-worker outcome and service measures (waits, abandonment) are what matter. A work-rate measure such as handling time per contact would also help, where studies report it.

## 5. How Varden and Halden were coded

- **Varden** contains one discretionary stratum and one coverage-bound stratum with opposite per-worker results. Was it entered as one study coded "mixed," or split into two entries? If pooled, its most informative contrast is lost. If split, the count isn't 23, and the two entries are correlated and need handling for that.
- **Halden** spans six sectors, including retail. How was it coded? And which estimate was used: the original 23.4% (manager-reported, scheduled hours) or Varga & Holm's corrected subset figures? The rule "use actual hours where reported" is ambiguous when actual hours exist only in a later re-analysis of a subset. Also confirm that the re-analysis wasn't entered as a separate study.

## 6. The rejection of Varga & Holm is half right

The controlled and actual-hours subgroups do address the measurement and selection arguments. On those grounds, "entirely an artifact" is not supported. But Varga & Holm's last argument was novelty, and the controlled studies are mostly short. Rebutting novelty requires the duration evidence, which (§1) can't bear the weight. A fair statement would be:

> Measurement and selection explain part, but not all, of the gain; whether the remainder persists is not yet established.

## 7. No formal risk-of-bias or certainty assessment

A registered systematic review would normally assess risk of bias study by study and grade the certainty of evidence:
- **Risk of bias:** RoB 2 for randomised trials, ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies.
- **Certainty:** GRADE.

Design is used as a moderator, but that isn't a substitute. Two "controlled" studies can differ hugely in quality. The paper also omits the reasons studies were excluded at full-text screening (the PRISMA flow), which is standard.

## Smaller points

- **Meta-regression.** Fitting three moderators (four parameters, since work type has three levels) to 23 studies is a lot. The "58% explained" figure is very imprecise at this k. The Limitations section acknowledges the small base; it should add that R² is unstable.
- **Sick leave.** "Fell in all 14 studies" is vote-counting. As in Varden, if schemes cut working days, sick *days* fall mechanically, so they should be counted per scheduled day.
- **Fatigue correlation.** r = 0.18 across 11 studies with different fatigue scales is an ecological correlation with almost no power. It can't distinguish a weak mechanism from a strong one. The paper is appropriately cautious about meetings; it should apply the same caution here.
- **Timesheet hours.** Even "actual hours" from timesheets miss unrecorded work, so the controlled and actual-hours estimates are probably still slightly overstated.
- **"Consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%)."** Low I² is not the same as every study agreeing. It would be better to say all seven point estimates were negative, if true.

## Overall

The central conclusion is well supported: per-hour gains are real but about half the headline figure, and per-worker output falls in coverage-bound work. The changes needed are:
- Remove "no sign of decay" from the abstract and results, and run a within-study analysis of decay.
- Report the controlled, actual-hours, record-based intersection as the best estimate, instead of claiming convergence across overlapping subgroups.
- Test whether the funnel asymmetry survives adjustment for the moderators.
- Reframe the per-hour result in coverage-bound work.
- State how Varden and Halden were entered.
- Add risk-of-bias and GRADE assessments.

I can draft revised abstract and Discussion text if that would help.
